# Kohut’s Place in American Judaism

This is the year in which we of the progressive school have been celebrating the centenary of Isaac M. Wise, the virtual father of American Reform. None the less, our survey of Judaism as a whole should be sufficiently comprehensive to realize the value of Kohut's contribution to the cause in making for a more positive Judaism. Let us not forget that Dr. Wise was a staunch pleader for the sanctity of Bible law, and that his views would be classed as conservative today. Dr. Kohut, then, prepared the way for that genius, Solomon Schechter, who "came and saw and conquered." But that is another story.

If he were alive today, he would see a different line of cleavage. There are two camps still, but no longer those of Orthodoxy and Reform, but of Zionism on the one hand and anti-Nationalism on the other. We are not as keen as were our fathers as to the discriminating points of distinction in synagogue observance—as to the covered head in worship, the recital of prayer in Hebrew—the retention of some Orientalisms. We realize that "life fulfills itself in many ways." The vital question is, Which school makes for the best kind of Jew? Something can be said for both wings. The motive behind the action is everything. This is the white of the elements. Its essence: within this, the actual essence is white, blue, and radiant like sweat, with poisonous white mustard seeds. This is the cause for the arising of the <term>nirmanakaya</term> <gloss>emanation body</gloss>. The mother's essence is like the flower of a grey horse <note>unclear botanical reference</note>, the size of a mustard seed, not radiant. Through the meeting of the two, like the mixing of curd and vermilion, they become a soft mass, a round mass, and an oblong mass. In the middle, because the mind of ignorance is enveloped, the fetus arises. Furthermore, if the six essences of the father and mother are mixed equally, that person will be born with strength, a beautiful form, great merit, and will be led by intelligence. If four are mixed equally, an average person is born. If three are mixed, a middle-average person. If two, a lower-average. If one, a commoner. If the father and mother's essences are not mixed equally, whether male or female is determined by previous accumulations. If one part father and two parts mother, it is a daughter. If two parts father and one part mother, it is a son. If equal but the father's essence is stronger, the person has little flesh but strong bones. If the mother's is stronger, they have much flesh and are very virtuous. If the essence and the dregs are mixed, a confused, foolish, or mute person will come. If the parents have a chronic illness, the child will have a disease. If the essences are of equal strength at the time of conception, a hermaphrodite will come. If the essences are incomplete...

...like one who performs a melt: for example, when performing a melt, if there is only fire and water, it will not melt; if the fire is too great, it will be consumed. Just as one adjusts the measure of the fire's heat, so too, at the time of entering into union with the <term>mudra</term>, if the conduct is too coarse, the <term>bindu</term> <gloss>vital essence</gloss> will wander and seek to escape. If it is not generated, bliss will be small, so generate it by adjusting the measure. Fix the awareness on each moment of bliss and remain in that bliss for a long time. If you cannot hold it, remain in the state of full awareness. Again, if you lose the bliss, generate it slowly, hold the bliss, and let it expand. By doing so, you will experience bliss and clarity. If you do not know these essential points, the <term>bindu</term> will escape and faults will arise. Third, being skillful in drawing up the <term>bindu</term> is like drawing water from a well: for example, if there is water at the bottom of a well, if it is not pulled up with a rope, it will not reach where the water is desired...

<leaf-break/>

...leaving activity in the state of the spontaneously present primordial purity, it is impossible not to capture it. If it is still not captured, block the path of the nectar's movement in the channels. If it is not captured thus, no qualities will arise, so one should persevere in the wind-yogas. Then, being skillful in distributing the <term>bindu</term> is like a generous donor distributing gifts: for example, a great universal monarch who gives gifts everywhere without hesitation—if he shows partiality, those people become angry. Similarly, if the yogi draws up the <term>bindu</term> but does not distribute it, faults will arise wherever it is not distributed. Therefore, guide the captured <term>bindu</term> to the joints of the body. First, send the <term>bindu</term> to the crown of the head, and as it stays there in a white mass, visualize it pervading all the channel-petals of the crown. Guide it with the seven physical movements. With the "laughing style of the <term>senmo</term> spirit," expel the wind three times. With the "gaze of the fox," inhale the wind three times. With the "churning method of the <term>tsame</term>," press down the upper wind and pull up the lower wind three times. With the "leaping of the wild animal," three times...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on maintaining vitality into old age. Having previously discussed more extreme measures like the consumption of blood, the author now pivots to the importance of proper digestion, environmental factors, and specific foods that promote "spirit" and longevity.</meta>

...[before the body] has digested, to take more nourishment distracts and fatigues nature; from which weariness, when frequently repeated, untimely old age arrives. In winter, let the elderly seek out sunny spots like sheep; in summer, let them revisit pleasant places and streams like birds. Let them frequently spend time among green and sweet-smelling plants. For these, being living and breathing, breathe forth to increase the spirit <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "spirit" was a subtle substance that connected the soul to the body, often replenished through scents and light.</note> of man. Indeed, let them flee to places generally friendly to bees. 

And let them taste honey in winter. For honey is a food primarily friendly to the elderly, except in cases where they fear the inflammation of bile <note>original: "bilis incendiũ" — Referring to the humoral theory where honey was considered "hot" and could aggravate a choleric or "bilious" temperament.</note>. Very fresh cheese is a friend. Dates are friends, as are figs, raisins, capers, sweet pomegranates, ginger, hyssop, scabious, and betony; but pistachios are much more so. 

However, pine nuts <note>original: "Pinei nuclei"</note> are the greatest [friends] of all, as we have previously stated. From these they will receive the most help, if they soak them for twelve hours in slightly warm water before they eat them. For in this way, they will not harm the stomach. Furthermore, while they use these, if they also dwell among pine groves, olive groves, and vines—or at least receive the vapor and scent of the pine—it will be beneficial. 

Likewise, let them often rub their bodies with the resin and "tears" <note>original: "lachrimoq" — This refers to the sap or resin that "weeps" from the bark of the tree, prized for its aromatic and medicinal properties.</note> of the pine, mixed with oil or wine. For it is probable that trees naturally endowed with long life—especially if they remain green even in winter—will benefit you toward a long life through their shade, their vapor, their fresh fruit, their wood, and any other timely use. We have spoken above about long-lived animals. Now indeed...

And yet even when he is angry, he does not act out of hatred or because he turns away from us. He does it so that, even in this way, he may draw us to himself. And they came to the other side of the sea, into the country of the Gadarenes.

2 And when he had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit,

5 And constantly, night and day, in the mountains and in the tombs, he was crying out and cutting himself with stones.

6 But seeing Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him,

10 And he pleaded with him earnestly not to send them out of the country.

Specifically, when the pie <note>original: "פשטידא" (pastida)</note> is covered, it is as if the hot bread and the house are covered. And [if it] secretes [juices], and the fat of the pie drips from the bread, such that its grease does not fall beneath the bread, then Rabbi Judah bar Meir HaKohen the Elder, the teacher of Rabbenu Gershom, Light of the Exile, ruled. He used to teach him [about] a <term>alpetin</term> <gloss>a type of cooking vessel or pie dish</gloss>, and he wished to prohibit even after the fact if one baked a Gentile's pie with that of an Israelite. However, we do not hold this way. And even those who say "the aroma is not a substance" <note>original: "ריחא לאו מילתא היא"</note>, it implies that with a pie, the oven [is] such that the aroma exits from there, and if it does not hinder the bread [it is fine]. And there are those who rule like Rav <note>original: "רב"</note> in the chapter <term>Kol HaBasar</term> <gloss>All Meat</gloss> [of the Talmud], that the aroma is a substance. And the whole passage there is understood according to him, and many Geonim <note>original: "גאונים" (leaders of the Babylonian academies)</note> disagreed on the matter. And Rabbi Ibn wrote that the custom is to be careful to arrange a cover for the pie when baking them with the bread. And so too for fillings. And any cover is not as if it were like hot bread and an open house [which] Rabbenu Gershom prohibited, and even with a cover it is prohibited initially because of the vent at the top. And there are those who bake a tube of egg <note>over</note> the vent at the top so that the aroma does not exit. And Rashi <note>original: "רש"י"</note> ruled in his [commentary] that it is permitted, and the Alfasi <note>original: "האלפס" (Rabbi Isaac Alfasi)</note> also ruled that it is permitted. And even according to Rav, he only prohibited meat of a slaughtered animal and meat of an animal that died of natural causes <term>nevelah</term> <gloss>carrion</gloss>, which absorb the aroma. And similarly, hot bread and an open house that has no ventilation to the right or to the left, but only through the bung hole...

<column-break/>

[He] does not hold like Rav Kahana, that bread baked with a roast is prohibited to eat with <term>kutaḥ</term> <gloss>a spicy dip made from sour milk or whey</gloss>. But all the world is accustomed to forbid baking a pie and a salted item together. But bread with another of them is permitted. And whoever is stringent, a blessing shall come upon him. One asked him about <term>ḥameẓ</term> <gloss>leaven</gloss> and <term>maẓah</term> <gloss>unleavened bread</gloss> that were baked together in one oven, and they permitted it. And if both aromas are understood in the Talmud, the aroma of bread is not understood. And many times we bake the pie with the bread, and we found regarding the breads of the thanksgiving offering that <term>ḥameẓ</term> and <term>maẓah</term> were baked together, that no Tanna <note>rabbinic teacher of the Mishnaic period</note> skipped [mentioning] it in the traditions of two ovens, or this one or that one [were] baked [separately]. In the chapter <term>Gid HaNasheh</term> <gloss>The Sciatic Nerve</gloss> we learned regarding milk, and it is prohibited to eat even from the dish until the milk permeates, even from below to above. And we conclude that it is like this thread, and since it is like a thread it does not hinder. And even if it were to permeate a little, it is nullified. Therefore, both [the piece] that is touching it and those [where] the membrane is upon it, if there is 60 [parts of permitted food to one of forbidden], they are permitted. And there are those who say that that piece upon which the membrane is, is permitted from that which was spilled, even if it does not have 60, since the membrane is there, it is prohibited only because of the milk that is upon it from the outside, and it does not permeate beyond the membrane to the piece to which the membrane is attached. And Rabbi Simeon of Kintz said: since the kid was feduş <note>original: "פדוש" (likely referring to being salted/pitted)</note>, if it was salted, the other pieces and the roast that fell...

<column-break/>

Even though there is not 60 there. And likewise, one must judge when the milk was salted upon the pieces that do not have 60 in them. That piece is entirely prohibited. [If] it was salted, the prohibition and the permitted [meat] together, therefore, my father, the Avi HaEzri <note>original: "אבי העזרי" (Rabbi Eliezer ben Joel HaLevi)</note>, ruled: milk and meat are judged like meat [with a] peeling [required] in the place where it touched the milk, and one must deepen the peeling more than that which it was <note>if</note> one salted the meat of a lean carcass with meat into which milk was absorbed, according to [one opinion] and [one] does not say "at the time it emits it does not absorb," but rather for this reason [the] Rav and the others say the bad [meat] is suitable to absorb into its interior and will absorb. And it is not established for us that all the pieces are prohibited, and it is not sufficient with a peeling, for that which is salted is like that which is hot, for that which is roasted, for the milk permeates from the head of the kid that went out in its milk; it is prohibited to eat even from the dish... this is not [so], for it is explained regarding the kid that went out in its milk, and he eats until he reaches the milk. And he answers: that is regarding this thread, [he] eats until he reaches the milk, meaning that we can estimate until where the milk permeates according to its scarcity, for example, if the milk was abundant and was permeating and dripping, even from the ear when it was a carcass. And so Rashi explained: when we found a kidney in milk, that is what is permitted, Rabbi Yoḥanan [said]: a kidney in milk, it is permitted because the membrane separates between them. 1. *Material:* because the material of the sugar of the ancients is honey and dew, whereas that of ours is the juice of a plant, which certainly differ from one another as plant and water. 2. *Form:* for Dioscorides and other ancient writers say that their sugar, as to its consistency and coagulation, is brittle like salt. Pliny even writes that it is white like gum. In contrast, before ours is boiled down, its color is rather blackish and yellowish than white, and it is not crushed with the teeth, but swallowed as a liquid. 3. *Efficient cause:* for with the sugar of the ancients, the night cold first thickens it, and then the arriving heat of the sun hardens it. But the primary efficient cause of our sugar is the plant itself; the secondary is the skilled heat of the fire, boiling and clarifying it, and finally reducing it into this conical shape that we see in wooden vessels. 4. *Place:* for the sugar of the ancients is born only in India and Arabia Felix on reeds and on their leaves. But ours grows in the islands of Sicily and the Canaries, where the flesh of the plant, similar in appearance only to a reed, contains that sugar. 5. *Use:* the sugar of the ancients, on Pliny's testimony, was adapted only for medical use. But ours is adapted for preparing the most delicious feasts, so much so that there is now no magnificent banquet that is not seasoned with much sugar. 6. *Virtues:* the sugar of the ancients, according to Dioscorides, is astringent to the bowels and useful for the stomach. But ours, as we know by experience, is suited rather to the chest than to the stomach. Furthermore, according to the testimony of Galen and Paul, their sugar does not cause thirst; that is, as Avicenna explains in Book 2, Chapter 757 of his *Canon*, it causes less thirst than honey. Ours, however, excites no less thirst than honey itself, which daily experience certainly confirms.

From that which we said belongs to the second kind, ours does not indeed differ in kind: for just as that was the juice of reeds, so also is ours. They differ nevertheless from one another in some respect, because the ancients for the most part pressed their sugar out of the reeds, although occasionally they also extracted it by boiling it down, as was shown above from Strabo, Statius, and others. Ours, however, is produced solely by boiling down. For the sugar canes, cut up into small pieces, are boiled down by the heat of the fire until the entire liquid, bubbling for a long time and consumed by the fire, thickens into sugar in the vessel like salt, hardens, and whitens. From this it is clear that the ancients were not ignorant of this method of boiling sugar down, but deliberately chose not to use it, perhaps because that pressed juice provided them with a most pleasant drink. They preferred therefore to use that liquid as a drink on account of its honey-sweetness, rather than reduce it by boiling with the heat of fire to the consistency and hardness of salt, as is customary today. But after the hope of profit taught the Indians to cut the reeds annually, and likewise taught the art and manner by which that liquid, after cutting those same reeds into small pieces and then boiling them down, could be reduced to the consistency of salt, it is likely that, enticed by that hope of profit, they ceased to use the pressed juice for drink. Or certainly, when they were unable to transport that uncorrupted juice to other and especially more distant regions, they wished to reduce it to the form that is imported today. Wherefore, since the sugar of the second kind among the ancients and our sugar, or that of the moderns, are gathered from the same reed, it cannot be that they differ in kind from one another. The wise one stirs up their own <term>samaya</term> <gloss>sacred pledge</gloss>.

<term>Oṃ hūṃ aṃ jrīṃ khaṃ</term>. <note>A string of seed syllables. They have no literal meaning; each is held to embody a sacred power.</note>

in the manner taught in the <term>Kalpa</term> <gloss>the ritual-procedure section of the tantra</gloss>.

neither crooked nor askew, but straight.
In this way the image is arranged beautifully.
If it is not done so, faults will arise.
Flowers, incense and likewise perfume,
lamps, garments and whatever else is available:
all of these, accompanied by mantras,
are to be offered to the deities,
with <term>Oṃ vajra puṣpe āḥ hūṃ</term> <gloss>"Oṃ, vajra flower, āḥ hūṃ"</gloss> and the like.
"This supreme flower,
born likewise from water and from dry land,
I offer to you with the highest faith.
Please accept it, each of you, as you wish.
This supreme incense,
arising from what is natural and what is compounded,
I offer with my faith.
Please accept it as you wish.
This supreme perfume,
arising from what is natural and what is compounded,
I offer with my faith.
Please accept it as you wish.
Destroyer of darkness, supreme among lights,
this lamp of butter and of sesame oil
I offer with faith,
so that true wisdom may spread.
Food and snacks in perfect abundance,
endowed with color, fragrance and taste,
a divine meal complete in every way:
I offer it; please accept it, each of you."
These and whatever else is at hand,
however little is available,
all of it is to be offered to the image
in due order, by this same <note>procedure</note>.
One prepares the <term>caru</term> <gloss>a cooked offering of grain</gloss> with mantric purity.
Then, with a stick made of gold,
one opens the eyes <note>of the image</note>. <note>The "eye-opening" is the climax of many consecration rites. The eyes are painted or touched with a golden stylus, and the image is then regarded as living and seeing.</note>
There the wise one offers food.

<term>Oṃ dhyāna samādhi prīṇane svāhā</term> <gloss>"Oṃ, to the one who delights in meditation and concentration, svāhā"</gloss>.
Having recited these, then once more
one leads the disciple fully inside <note>the maṇḍala</note> <note>and says:</note>
"The images which you requested of me,
in particular, through the consecration as it is taught,
I have accomplished their purpose…"

# On the Nature of the Soul and Spirit

In the treatise *On the Soul and the Spirit* <note>original: "de anim. & spirit."</note>, it is established that the distinction between these faculties is essential for understanding human nature.

Aristotle, in his *Book on the Spirit* <note>original: "lib. de spiritu"</note>, asserts that there are spirits <note>original: "esse spiritus"</note> which act as the primary instruments of the soul's power within the physical body.

In the *Theological Resolutions* <note>original: "Resolut. Theolog."</note>, it is further clarified that, insofar as the soul looks toward higher things, it is called the **intellect**; insofar as it looks toward lower things, it is called **reason**. <note>original: "quod, quatenus anima respicit altiora, dicitur intellectus, quatenus inferiora, ratio."</note>

The intellect of the foul <note>original: "fedi"; likely referring to the corrupted or base state of the mind</note> must be purified to perceive divine truths.

The physical seat of these movements often involves the **diaphragm** <term>diaphragma</term> <note>the muscular partition between the chest and abdomen, historically believed to be a center of emotion or "spirit"</note>, which regulates the vital breath.

Through the wild bearing <note>original: "ferationem"; referring to a state of wildness or animalistic impulse</note> of the passions, the spirit can become clouded, losing its orientation toward the higher intellect.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchical definitions of the soul, distinguishing between the intellect (focused on the divine) and reason (focused on the mundane), while noting the physiological role of the diaphragm.</summary>
